techniques.name: Cross-Modal Consistency Scoring
techniques.description: Cross-modal consistency scoring checks whether content in one modality matches content in another, such as an image and its caption, a generated image and the prompt that produced it, or an audio clip and its description. It uses a contrastively trained model, one that has learned from large collections of paired examples to turn each item into an embedding (a numerical vector describing its content) and to place matching pairs close together: CLIP, trained on image-caption pairs, for images and text, or CLAP, its audio-and-text counterpart, for audio and text. The score for a pair is the cosine similarity of its two embeddings; in the standard image form, CLIPScore, negative similarities are set to zero and the result is rescaled, and no human-written reference is needed. A practitioner scores every pair in an evaluation set or in production, sets a threshold against a sample of human judgements, and then compares average scores between systems or sends pairs below the threshold for review. The score shows whether two items are about the same things, not whether every detail of a description is correct.

example_use_cases.description: A public library deploying an automatic alt-text generator for its digitised photograph collection scores every generated description against its image and routes those below a threshold, set on a sample rated by staff, to a cataloguer, so that descriptions of the wrong subject are caught before visitors using screen readers meet them; names, dates and places in the descriptions are checked separately.

A design-software company deciding whether to ship a new version of its text-to-image model generates images for the same few thousand varied prompts with fixed random seeds, compares the average image-prompt scores of the old and new versions, and checks the comparison against human ratings on a subset before release.

A team assembling an image-caption training set from web data drops pairs whose image-text similarity falls below a threshold, as the builders of LAION-5B did, and audits a sample of the discarded pairs by subject and demographic group before accepting the filter, because such filters remove some groups' images at higher rates.

A broadcaster's archive team generating text descriptions for an untagged sound-effects library scores each description against its clip with an audio-text model, uses the scores only to order clips for human listening checks rather than to accept descriptions automatically, and records the agreement between scores and listeners' judgements.

limitations.description: Contrastively trained image-text models largely ignore word order, relations between objects and which attribute belongs to which object, so a description that names the right things in the wrong relationship can score almost as well as a correct one. The score checks that the right content is mentioned, not that the description of how it fits together is right.

It cannot check what is not visible or audible. Names, places, events and other context in a news photograph or an archive recording are outside what the encoder can match, and the original authors found the image score weaker than reference-based metrics on news captions, so it should not be the only check where such facts matter.

Scores inherit the encoder's training data, which is mostly web alt-text, and its biases. An audit of CLIP-based filtering found that data associated with LGBTQ+ people, older women and younger men was excluded at higher rates, so a single threshold can be stricter for some subjects than others and needs checking by group.

Scores have no absolute meaning: they depend on the encoder checkpoint and on the tool's scaling (the original CLIPScore multiplies the cosine similarity by 2.5, torchmetrics by 100), so values are not comparable across checkpoints or tools. The default CLIP text encoder also reads at most 77 tokens, so longer descriptions are judged on their opening only. Thresholds must be set and reported for the specific model and settings used.

The audio form is weaker still: CLAP-based scores have been found to correlate only weakly with human ratings of how well audio matches its text, so for audio the score is a coarse screen to prioritise human checks rather than evidence of consistency on its own.

resources.title: CLIPScore: A Reference-free Evaluation Metric for Image Captioning
resources.abstract: Image captioning has conventionally relied on reference-based automatic evaluations, where machine captions are compared against captions written by humans.This is in contrast to the reference-free manner in which humans assess caption quality.In this paper, we report the surprising empirical finding that CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), a cross-modal model pretrained on 400M im-age+caption pairs from the web, can be used for robust automatic evaluation of image captioning without the need for references.Experiments spanning several corpora demonstrate that our new reference-free metric, CLIPScore, achieves the highest correlation with human judgements, outperforming existing reference-based metrics like CIDEr and SPICE.Information gain experiments demonstrate that CLIPScore, with its tight focus on image-text compatibility, is complementary to existing reference-based metrics that emphasize text-text similarities.Thus, we also present a reference-augmented version, RefCLIPScore, which achieves even higher correlation.Beyond literal description tasks, several case studies reveal domains where CLIPScore performs well (clip-art images, alt-text rating), but also where it is relatively weaker in comparison to reference-based metrics, e.g., news captions that require richer contextual knowledge.

Who's in and who's out? A case study of multimodal CLIP-filtering in DataComp
resources.abstract: As training datasets become increasingly drawn from unstructured, uncontrolled environments such as the web, researchers and industry practitioners have increasingly relied upon data filtering techniques to “filter out the noise” of web-scraped data. While datasets have been widely shown to reflect the biases and values of their creators, in this paper we contribute to an emerging body of research that assesses the filters used to create these datasets. We show that image-text data filtering also has biases and is value-laden, encoding specific notions of what is counted as “high-quality” data. In our work, we audit a standard approach of image-text CLIP-filtering on the academic benchmark DataComp’s CommonPool by analyzing discrepancies of filtering through various annotation techniques across multiple modalities of image, text, and website source. We find that data relating to several imputed demographic groups — such as LGBTQ+ people, older women, and younger men — are associated with higher rates of exclusion. We also find prevalence of Western bias, where the CLIP filter is more likely to include data related to Western countries compared to that of non-Western countries. Moreover, we demonstrate cases of exclusion amplification: not only are certain marginalized groups already underrepresented in the unfiltered data, but CLIP-filtering excludes data from these groups at higher rates. The data-filtering step in the machine learning pipeline can therefore exacerbate representation disparities already present in the data-gathering step, especially when existing filters are designed to optimize a specifically-chosen downstream performance metric like zero-shot image classification accuracy. Finally, we show that the NSFW filter fails to remove sexually-explicit content from CommonPool, and that CLIP-filtering includes several categories of copyrighted content at high rates. Our conclusions point to a need for fundamental changes in dataset creation and filtering practices. Content warning: This paper discusses societal stereotypes and sexually-explicit material that may be disturbing, distressing, and/or offensive to the reader.

techniques.name: Synthetic Data Evaluation
techniques.description: Synthetic data evaluation checks whether an artificial dataset made to stand in for sensitive real records is safe to share and still useful, and reports the trade-off between the two. Privacy is tested by simulating an attacker who holds the synthetic data and some facts about a person, and measuring how accurately the attacker can use the data to infer that person's sensitive values. Fidelity is tested by comparing the synthetic and real data column by column and in pairs of columns. Another check trains a classifier to tell the two apart, and a classifier that cannot beat chance suggests they are statistically alike. Utility is tested by running the analyses or training the models the data is meant for on the synthetic data and comparing the results with those from the real data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research office wants to share synthetic outpatient records with university partners. Before release it simulates an attacker who knows each patient's age band, sex and postcode district and tries to infer their diagnosis from the synthetic table, and it withholds the data if the attack does better than guessing from overall diagnosis rates.

A national statistics office gives researchers synthetic microdata for exploratory analysis. After the researchers settle on their models, the office runs the same models on the real data inside a secure environment and compares the estimates, to tell the researchers whether their exploratory conclusions can be trusted.

A bank's fraud team generates synthetic card transactions to share with an external vendor. It compares how often each fraud type appears and how amount, merchant type and time of day relate in the real and synthetic data, then checks that a model trained on the synthetic data still catches rare fraud in held-out real transactions.

limitations.description: Stronger privacy protection usually costs data quality, so the three scores pull against each other. There is no neutral threshold: where to set the balance depends on how sensitive the data is and what it will be used for, and the evaluation reports the trade-off without settling it.

Attack-based privacy tests only probe the attacks and attacker knowledge that were tried. A dataset that resists them may still leak to an attacker with more auxiliary information or a better method, so a good result is not proof of safety.

Fidelity and utility scores depend on which metrics, models and analyses are chosen. A synthetic dataset can match the real data on the columns and column pairs checked yet differ in ways that matter for a particular analysis, and general and analysis-specific utility scores can disagree.

Scores summarise the whole table, so rare events and small subgroups can be lost without moving the totals much. A fraud pattern or a minority group that the generator has smoothed away may show up only if the evaluation is designed to look for it.

The tests need statistical, privacy-engineering and domain expertise to set up and read. A classifier-based fidelity check can be misled by over-fitting or under-fitting the classifier, and weak settings can make poor synthetic data look good.

resources.title: General and Specific Utility Measures for Synthetic Data
resources.abstract: Data holders can produce synthetic versions of data sets when concerns about potential disclosure restrict the availability of the original records. The paper is concerned with methods to judge whether such synthetic data have a distribution that is comparable with that of the original data: what we term general utility. We consider how general utility compares with specific utility: the similarity of results of analyses from the synthetic data and the original data. We adapt a previous general measure of data utility, the propensity score mean-squared error pMSE, to the specific case of synthetic data and derive its distribution for the case when the correct synthesis model is used to create the synthetic data. Our asymptotic results are confirmed by a simulation study. We also consider two specific utility measures, confidence interval overlap and standardized difference in summary statistics, which we compare with the general utility results. We present two contrasting examples of data syntheses: one illustrating synthetic data that is evaluated as being useful by both general and specific measures and the second where neither is the case. For the second case we show how the general utility measures can identify the deficiencies of the synthetic data and suggest how this can inform possible improvements to the synthesis method.

A Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic electronic health record generation models
resources.abstract: Synthetic health data have the potential to mitigate privacy concerns in supporting biomedical research and healthcare applications. Modern approaches for data generation continue to evolve and demonstrate remarkable potential. Yet there is a lack of a systematic assessment framework to benchmark methods as they emerge and determine which methods are most appropriate for which use cases. In this work, we introduce a systematic benchmarking framework to appraise key characteristics with respect to utility and privacy metrics. We apply the framework to evaluate synthetic data generation methods for electronic health records data from two large academic medical centers with respect to several use cases. The results illustrate that there is a utility-privacy tradeoff for sharing synthetic health data and further indicate that no method is unequivocally the best on all criteria in each use case, which makes it evident why synthetic data generation methods need to be assessed in context.

resources.title: Generating and Evaluating Synthetic UK Primary Care Data: Preserving Data Utility & Patient Privacy
resources.abstract: There is increasing interest in the potential of synthetic data to validate and benchmark machine learning algorithms as well as reveal any biases in real-world data used for algorithm development. This paper discusses the key requirements of synthetic data for such purposes and proposes an approach to generating and evaluating synthetic data that meets these requirements. We propose a framework to generate and evaluate synthetic data with the aim of simultaneously preserving the complexities of ground truth data in the synthetic data whilst also ensuring privacy. We include as a case study, a proof-of-concept synthetic dataset modelled on UK primary care data to demonstrate the application of this framework.

techniques.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Evaluation
techniques.description: A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system answers a question by retrieving passages from a document collection and asking a language model to write an answer from them. RAG evaluation scores retrieval on whether the fetched passages are relevant and focused and, where reference answers exist, whether they contain what the answer needs. Generation is scored on faithfulness, usually by splitting the answer into individual claims and reporting the share that the fetched passages support, and on answer relevance, which asks whether the answer addresses the question. Frameworks such as Ragas automate these checks with a second language model acting as judge, so faithfulness and relevance need no human-written reference answers. Test sets can also include questions the documents cannot answer, to check that the system says so instead of guessing.

example_use_cases.description: A software company's support team tests its troubleshooting assistant on a set of real customer questions. For each answer it checks that the retrieved pages are the right ones and that every configuration step or command quoted appears in the official documentation, and it holds back changes that introduce invented steps.

A law firm's research team tests an assistant that summarises case law from its own database. Each summary is split into claims and each claim is checked against the passages the assistant retrieved, and summaries with unsupported claims are flagged for review before the assistant is rolled out to fee-earners.

A hospital pharmacy team tests a clinical decision-support tool that retrieves guidelines and patient records. A clinician compares each generated treatment suggestion with the retrieved guideline text, and the team tracks the share of suggestions that go beyond what the sources say before the tool reaches ward staff.

A benefits agency tests its eligibility chatbot on questions drawn from real enquiries, including some the policy documents cannot answer. It checks that quoted amounts and rules match the retrieved policy text and that the chatbot says it cannot answer instead of guessing, before the chatbot is opened to citizens.

limitations.description: Scores that judge retrieval against known answers, such as context recall, need reference answers or labelled passages, which are slow to write and need experts in specialist domains. Reference-free scores avoid this but only penalise irrelevant passages, so they cannot show that a needed passage was never retrieved.

Scores usually come from a second language model acting as judge, so they inherit its errors and its sensitivity to wording. In the original Ragas study the judge agreed with human raters in 95% of pairwise comparisons on faithfulness but only 70% on context relevance, and it struggled to pick out the key sentences in long contexts.

Faithfulness measures whether an answer is supported by the retrieved text, not whether that text is correct, current or complete. A system that retrieves an outdated document and reports it accurately scores well, so the knowledge base needs checking separately.

Claim-by-claim checking may not catch answers that chain reasoning across several documents. Misleading emphasis, selective quotation and unsupported leaps between sources can pass when each sentence is individually supported, so these cases need targeted test questions and human review.

When a score is low, the cause can lie in retrieval, in generation or in how the two interact, and the scores alone often cannot say which. Diagnosis usually needs manual inspection of the retrieved passages and answers for a sample of failing questions.

resources.title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
resources.abstract: We introduce RAGAs (Retrieval Augmented Generation Assessment), a framework for reference-free evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines. RAGAs is available at [https://github.com/explodinggradients/ragas]. RAG systems are composed of a retrieval and an LLM based generation module. They provide LLMs with knowledge from a reference textual database, enabling them to act as a natural language layer between a user and textual databases, thus reducing the risk of hallucinations. Evaluating RAG architectures is challenging due to several dimensions to consider: the ability of the retrieval system to identify relevant and focused context passages, the ability of the LLM to exploit such passages faithfully, and the quality of the generation itself. With RAGAs, we introduce a suite of metrics that can evaluate these different dimensions without relying on ground truth human annotations. We posit that such a framework can contribute crucially to faster evaluation cycles of RAG architectures, which is especially important given the fast adoption of LLMs.

resources.title: Enhancing the Precision and Interpretability of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) in Legal Technology: A Survey
resources.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a promising solution that can enhance the capabilities of large language model (LLM) applications in critical domains, including legal technology, by retrieving knowledge from external databases. Implementing RAG pipelines requires careful attention to the techniques and methods implemented in the different stages of the RAG process. However, robust RAG can enhance LLM generation with faithfulness and few hallucinations in responses. In this paper, we discuss the application of RAG in the legal domain. First, we present an overview of the main RAG methods, stages, techniques, and applications in the legal domain. We then briefly discuss the different information retrieval models, processes, and applied methods in current legal RAG solutions. Then, we explain the different quantitative and qualitative evaluation metrics. We also describe several emerging datasets and benchmarks. We then discuss and assess the ethical and privacy considerations for legal RAG and summarize various challenges, and propose a challenge scale based on RAG failure points and control over external knowledge. Finally, we provide insights into promising future research to leverage RAG efficiently and effectively in the legal field.

resources.title: ASTRID - An Automated and Scalable TRIaD for the Evaluation of RAG-based Clinical Question Answering Systems
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive potential in clinical question answering (QA), with Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) emerging as a leading approach for ensuring the factual accuracy of model responses.However, current automated RAG metrics perform poorly in clinical and conversational use cases.Using clinical human evaluations of responses is expensive, unscalable, and not conducive to the continuous iterative development of RAG systems.To address these challenges, we introduce ASTRID -an Automated and Scalable TRIaD for evaluating clinical QA systems leveraging RAG -consisting of three metrics: Context Relevance (CR), Refusal Accuracy (RA), and Conversational Faithfulness (CF).Our novel evaluation metric, CF, is designed to better capture the faithfulness of a model's response to the knowledge base without penalizing conversational elements.Additionally, our metric RA captures the refusal to address questions outside of the system's scope of practice.To validate our triad, we curate a dataset of over 200 real-world patient questions posed to an LLM-based QA agent during surgical follow-up for cataract surgery -the highest volume operation in the worldaugmented with clinician-selected questions for emergency, and clinical and non-clinical out-of-domain scenarios.We demonstrate that CF predicts human ratings of faithfulness more accurately than existing definitions in conversational settings.Furthermore, using eight different LLMs, we demonstrate that the three metrics can closely agree with human evaluations, highlighting the potential of these metrics for use in LLM-driven automated evaluation pipelines.Finally, we show that evaluation using our triad of CF, RA, and CR exhibits alignment with clinician assessment for inappropriate, harmful, or unhelpful responses.We also publish the prompts and datasets for these experiments, providing valuable resources for further research and development.

techniques.name: Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics
techniques.description: Bootstrap confidence intervals put a range around a model's measured performance, showing how much the score could differ had another test set of the same size been drawn from the same population. The labelled held-out evaluation set is resampled with replacement thousands of times, each resample holding as many cases as the original so that some cases appear more than once and others not at all, and the metric (an error rate, the area under a curve, a translation score) is recomputed on each resample from the model's stored predictions, with no retraining. The spread of these recomputed values stands in for the sampling distribution of the metric: the percentile interval takes its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles for a 95 per cent interval, and the bias-corrected and accelerated (BCa) interval shifts those percentiles to correct for bias and skew in that distribution. The statistic can also be the difference between two models scored on the same cases, recomputed on each shared resample, which shows whether an observed improvement is larger than the noise from test-set sampling. The result is the metric with lower and upper bounds at a stated confidence level, so a requirement such as a maximum false-positive rate can be checked against the bound rather than the point estimate.

example_use_cases.description: A medical-imaging company preparing a regulatory submission reports its fracture detector's sensitivity and specificity at the locked threshold with 95 per cent bootstrap intervals. Because each patient contributes several radiographs, it resamples patients rather than images, so the interval reflects the number of independent patients in the test set rather than the larger number of images.

A machine-translation team deciding whether to replace its production model scores the current and candidate systems on the same held-out sentences, recomputes the difference in BLEU score on 1,000 shared bootstrap resamples of those sentences, and approves the change only if the 95 per cent interval for the difference lies above zero.

A fisheries agency whose vessel-detection model must keep false alarms below 2 per cent of non-vessel image patches re-measures the false-positive rate each quarter on several thousand newly labelled patches, puts a bootstrap interval on it, and states compliance against the interval's upper bound. In a quarter where the labelled sample yields only a handful of false positives, the agency uses an exact binomial interval instead, because the bootstrap interval is too narrow at that count.

An evaluation team comparing two large language models on a 500-question internal benchmark reports each model's accuracy with a BCa bootstrap interval and puts a paired interval on the difference, which shows that a 1.5-point lead is within the sampling noise of a test set that size, so the team does not cite it as evidence that one model is better.

limitations.description: For a rate built from rare errors, such as a low false-positive rate, the interval is too narrow when the test set holds only a handful of errors. With 200 negatives and a true rate of 0.5 per cent, about a third of test sets have no false positives; the percentile interval is then [0, 0] and BCa may return no value. For a single proportion the exact binomial (Clopper-Pearson) interval avoids this; the bootstrap earns its place on metrics with no simple formula.

Resampling single cases assumes they are independent. When several test cases come from one patient, vessel, user or time window, their errors are correlated, and resampling cases treats them as separate evidence, giving intervals that can be much too narrow. Resampling whole clusters (patients, days) instead restores the right width when there are enough clusters, which needs the cluster of each case to be recorded in the test set; with few clusters the interval is again too narrow.

The interval reflects only which cases happened to be in the test set. It says nothing about variation from retraining the model on other data or with another random seed, nor about whether the test set represents the deployment population, so a narrow interval on an unrepresentative test set is precise and still wrong. Uncertainty in a single prediction, from retraining on resampled training data, is a different procedure; see Bootstrap Ensembles.

If the decision threshold, the model or the metric was chosen by looking at the same test set, resampling that set leaves the interval centred on an optimistic estimate, because the selection effect is not reproduced in the resamples. The choice has to be made on data separate from the set that is resampled.

Coverage is approximate and improves with test-set size. Percentile intervals can be too narrow on small test sets, and more so for skewed metrics; the BCa interval corrects for bias and skew but not for the narrowness that comes from a small test set, so small test sets stay a problem. BCa also needs an extra leave-one-out pass over the test set, which is slow for large sets or costly metrics, and it returns no interval when every resample gives the same value.

resources.title: Bootstrap Methods: Another Look at the Jackknife
resources.abstract: We discuss the following problem: given a random sample X = (X1, X2, …, Xn) from an unknown probability distribution F, estimate the sampling distribution of some prespecified random variable R(X, F), on the basis of the observed data x. (Standard jackknife theory gives an approximate mean and variance in the case R(X, F) = θ(F̂) − θ(F), θ some parameter of interest.) A general method, called the "bootstrap," is introduced, and shown to work satisfactorily on a variety of estimation problems. The jackknife is shown to be a linear approximation method for the bootstrap. The exposition proceeds by a series of examples: variance of the sample median, error rates in a linear discriminant analysis, ratio estimation, estimating regression parameters, etc.

resources.title: Better Bootstrap Confidence Intervals
resources.abstract: We consider the problem of setting approximate confidence intervals for a single parameter θ in a multiparameter family. The standard approximate intervals based on maximum likelihood theory, , can be quite misleading. In practice, tricks based on transformations, bias corrections, and so forth, are often used to improve their accuracy. The bootstrap confidence intervals discussed in this article automatically incorporate such tricks without requiring the statistician to think them through for each new application, at the price of a considerable increase in computational effort. The new intervals incorporate an improvement over previously suggested methods, which results in second-order correctness in a wide variety of problems. In addition to parametric families, bootstrap intervals are also developed for nonparametric situations.

techniques.name: Operating-Point ROC Analysis
techniques.description: Operating-point ROC analysis measures how often a classifier makes each kind of mistake at the decision threshold it will actually use, which is the evidence behind claims such as 'the false-positive rate stays within acceptable bounds'. A classifier that outputs a score is turned into a yes-or-no decision by a threshold, and moving the threshold trades one kind of error against the other. On a labelled held-out set, the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots the true-positive rate (the share of actual positives that are flagged, also called sensitivity) against the false-positive rate (the share of actual negatives wrongly flagged, equal to one minus specificity) at every possible threshold; the operating threshold is then chosen from the curve to meet a stated limit on one error rate or to minimise the expected cost of errors, or an existing threshold is confirmed. At that one threshold the analysis reports the confusion matrix (the counts of true positives, false positives, false negatives and true negatives) and the false-positive and false-negative rates with their complements, specificity and sensitivity. The output is a set of error rates tied to a named threshold and a named test set, against which a requirement on error rates can be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital's clinical informatics team evaluating a vendor's sepsis alert scores a year of its own admissions, plots the ROC curve and fixes the alert threshold its operations committee chose from the vendor's recommended range. At that threshold it reports sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value and the share of all admissions that would trigger an alert, and uses the false-positive count and alert volume to decide whether ward staff can act on the alerts.

A card-payments company re-runs the analysis every month on transactions its fraud analysts have labelled, confirms that the false-positive rate at the live threshold is still under the limit agreed with its customer-service team, and, whenever the rate has drifted above that limit, reopens the threshold choice on the latest ROC curve and confirms the new threshold on the following month's labelled sample.

A manufacturer's quality engineers choose the threshold for a visual-inspection model by weighing the cost of scrapping a good part against the cost of shipping a defective one, using the ROC curve and the line's defect rate, then report the false-reject and defect-escape rates that the chosen threshold gives on a separate held-out production batch.

A rail operator's safety team assessing a camera-based obstacle detector for level crossings sets the decision threshold on a tuning set so that the miss rate meets the requirement allocated to the detector. It then measures the false-negative rate at that threshold on a separate set of recorded crossings, broken down into daylight, night and rain, and enters the confusion matrices in the safety case as verification evidence.

limitations.description: The rates are evidence only if they are measured on labelled cases that played no part in choosing the threshold. A threshold set to give a 1 per cent false-positive rate on a tuning set gives exactly that rate there by construction, and with a few hundred negative tuning cases its true rate on new data can be half as high again. Choosing the threshold on one set and reporting rates on another, or nesting the choice inside cross-validation, avoids this at the cost of more labelled data.

False-positive and true-positive rates do not change with how common the positive class is, but the share of alerts that are correct does. A false-positive rate within its limit can still mean most alerts are false when the condition is rare: at 90 per cent sensitivity and a 5 per cent false-positive rate, only about 15 per cent of alerts are correct when 1 case in 100 is positive. Claims about alert burden need the positive predictive value at the deployment prevalence as well.

A rate from a finite test set is an estimate, and with few negatives or few errors it can fall well below the true rate by chance. A claim that a rate is within a limit needs a confidence interval (exact binomial for a single rate; see Bootstrap Confidence Intervals for Evaluation Metrics for other metrics) narrower than the margin to the limit. With no misses, about 3,000 positives show a miss rate below 1 in 1,000, and 30,000 below 1 in 10,000, at 95 per cent confidence.

The threshold is a fixed score, so the rates hold only while the scores for each class stay as in the test set. A new scanner, fraud pattern or patient mix shifts the scores and moves the false-positive rate with no change to the model, so the analysis must be repeated on labelled operational samples, which can be slow or costly. Labels matter too: where only flagged cases are reviewed, the rate for unflagged cases is unknown unless a random sample of them is labelled.

A single rate averages over the whole test set. It can meet its limit overall while exceeding it for a group of people or an operating condition (night-time images, one hospital site) that is rare in the test data. Rates need reporting for each group and condition the claim covers, each with enough cases to be informative, which can multiply the labelled data required.

resources.title: External Validation of a Widely Implemented Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model in Hospitalized Patients
resources.abstract: Importance: The Epic Sepsis Model (ESM), a proprietary sepsis prediction model, is implemented at hundreds of US hospitals. The ESM's ability to identify patients with sepsis has not been adequately evaluated despite widespread use. Objective: To externally validate the ESM in the prediction of sepsis and evaluate its potential clinical value compared with usual care. Design, Setting, and Participants: This retrospective cohort study was conducted among 27 697 patients aged 18 years or older admitted to Michigan Medicine, the academic health system of the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, with 38 455 hospitalizations between December 6, 2018, and October 20, 2019. Exposure: The ESM score, calculated every 15 minutes. Main Outcomes and Measures: Sepsis, as defined by a composite of (1) the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention surveillance criteria and (2) International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision diagnostic codes accompanied by 2 systemic inflammatory response syndrome criteria and 1 organ dysfunction criterion within 6 hours of one another. Model discrimination was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve at the hospitalization level and with prediction horizons of 4, 8, 12, and 24 hours. Model calibration was evaluated with calibration plots. The potential clinical benefit associated with the ESM was assessed by evaluating the added benefit of the ESM score compared with contemporary clinical practice (based on timely administration of antibiotics). Alert fatigue was evaluated by comparing the clinical value of different alerting strategies. Results: We identified 27 697 patients who had 38 455 hospitalizations (21 904 women [57%]; median age, 56 years [interquartile range, 35-69 years]) meeting inclusion criteria, of whom sepsis occurred in 2552 (7%). The ESM had a hospitalization-level area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.63 (95% CI, 0.62-0.64). The ESM identified 183 of 2552 patients with sepsis (7%) who did not receive timely administration of antibiotics, highlighting the low sensitivity of the ESM in comparison with contemporary clinical practice. The ESM also did not identify 1709 patients with sepsis (67%) despite generating alerts for an ESM score of 6 or higher for 6971 of all 38 455 hospitalized patients (18%), thus creating a large burden of alert fatigue. Conclusions and Relevance: This external validation cohort study suggests that the ESM has poor discrimination and calibration in predicting the onset of sepsis. The widespread adoption of the ESM despite its poor performance raises fundamental concerns about sepsis management on a national level.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.

techniques.name: SMACTR Internal Algorithmic Audit
techniques.description: SMACTR is an internal audit procedure for AI systems, proposed by Raji and colleagues in 2020, in which an audit team inside the developing organisation but separate from the product team examines a system during development and before launch against the ethical objectives and requirements the organisation has declared for it. The audit runs in five stages, each producing set documents. In Scoping, auditors review the product requirements and the declared objectives and write an ethical review of the use case, drawing in independent domain experts and marginalised groups, and a social impact assessment; in Mapping, they map the people involved, review existing design records, interview the engineers and begin a failure modes and effects analysis (FMEA), a systematic review of the foreseeable ways the system could fail and their effects, used to rank risks for testing. In Artefact Collection, a checklist confirms that the expected development documents, such as model cards and datasheets, exist; in Testing, auditors run tests chosen from the FMEA's priorities, such as adversarial probing with tailored inputs, and rate each risk high, mid or low from its likelihood and severity in an ethical risk analysis chart; in Reflection, they set the results against the declared objectives, finalise the risk analysis and agree a remediation plan with the engineering team. The documents are kept in an algorithmic design history file, from which the auditors write a summary report that leadership can use to decide whether the system launches, changes or is abandoned.

example_use_cases.description: An insurer's internal audit team audits a claims-triage model before launch. Interviews in Mapping reveal that a field used as a proxy for chronic illness was dropped late without the requirements being updated; the FMEA ranks under-prioritising complex claims as the top risk, so Testing concentrates on claims from people with several conditions, and the summary report goes to the risk committee with a remediation plan and a recommendation to delay launch.

A software company's responsible-AI audit team audits a customer-support chatbot. Artefact Collection finds no datasheet for the fine-tuning conversations, so the auditors require the product team to write one before testing; prompts drawn from the FMEA then test whether the bot discloses other customers' account details or gives poorer answers to customers writing in non-standard English, and the ethical risk chart and remediation plan record what must change before release.

A government digital service's audit team, which reports to the agency's chief risk officer rather than to the delivery programme, audits an in-house model that prioritises housing repair requests before it replaces manual triage. The chief risk officer uses the summary report to decide whether the model goes live, and the design history file and report are filed where the agency's external auditors and ombudsman can later inspect them.

limitations.description: The auditors are employees of the organisation they audit and share its interests; the authors acknowledge that independence is hard to keep and that audits risk becoming reputation management. Findings carry more weight when the audit team reports outside the product's management line and the design history file can be examined by an outside party.

The system is judged against the ethical objectives the organisation declares for it, which the authors note have been criticised as vague, and the paper leaves open what level of performance, for example how close to parity across groups, counts as acceptable. A clean audit shows consistency with the standards and thresholds the organisation chose to declare, and says nothing about any external standard it did not adopt.

The Testing stage prescribes no particular tests; the authors expect tests to vary widely by system and to follow the FMEA's priorities. What the audit can show about the system's behaviour therefore depends on the tests the team chooses, and a failure mode the FMEA did not foresee is likely to go untested.

The audit is deliberately slow and document-heavy, and the authors note that fast, iterative development is hard to audit. Its results describe the system at the time of the audit, so a model retrained or reconfigured afterwards is not covered unless the relevant stages are repeated.

The paper does not say which systems should be audited or in how much depth, leaving that to the organisation, and it illustrates the procedure only on two hypothetical client projects. Published evidence of how well it finds problems in real systems is limited.

techniques.name: Continuous Ranked Probability Score
techniques.description: The continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) measures the quality of a probabilistic forecast of a numerical quantity, such as tomorrow's temperature or next week's demand, by scoring the whole predicted distribution, not just a single best guess, against the value later observed. For each case it compares the forecast's cumulative distribution (the predicted probability that the outcome will fall below each possible value) with a step that jumps from 0 to 1 at the observed value, squares the gap at every value and adds these up, which is the same as adding up the Brier score of the yes-or-no forecasts 'the outcome will be below this value' over every possible threshold. For a forecast given as an ensemble or a sample it can be computed as the average distance between the members and the observation minus half the average distance between pairs of members, closed forms exist for common distributions such as the Gaussian, and for a single-value forecast it reduces to the absolute error, so probabilistic and deterministic forecasts can be compared directly. The score is proper: a forecaster expects the best score by reporting the distribution they actually believe, so it cannot be improved on average by making forecasts narrower or wider than warranted, and it is lowest when the forecast distribution matches how outcomes actually vary. Scores are averaged over many cases, are in the units of the forecast quantity with lower values better, and are often reported as a skill score relative to a reference forecast such as climatology (the long-run historical distribution), giving evidence for claims about the accuracy of a forecaster's probabilities by variable, location and lead time.

example_use_cases.description: A national weather service deciding whether to run a machine-learning ensemble alongside its physics-based ensemble scores both against a year of station observations, computing the fair CRPS (the two ensembles differ in size) for 2-metre temperature and 10-metre wind at every station and lead time. It adopts the new system only for the variables and lead times where its CRPS skill relative to the existing ensemble is positive.

A wind-farm operator choosing between two vendors of probabilistic power forecasts for day-ahead trading receives 19 quantiles per hour from each. It approximates each forecast's CRPS by averaging the quantile scores across those levels and compares the vendors over a full winter against metered output. Because high-output hours drive balancing costs, it also compares them on a version of the score weighted towards the upper quantiles, averaged over all hours, not only those with high output.

A hospital group's capacity team plans elective admissions with a probabilistic forecast of bed occupancy one week ahead. Each week it computes the forecast's CRPS against the occupancy that followed and its skill score against a seasonal naive forecast, and a rolling eight-week skill score below zero triggers a review of the model before it is used for the next planning cycle.

limitations.description: One CRPS value combines calibration (whether outcomes behave like draws from the forecast distribution) and sharpness (how narrow the forecast is), so a better score does not show which improved, and an average over many cases can hide conditions in which forecasts are consistently too narrow or too wide. A claim about calibration needs Hersbach's decomposition of the score into reliability and resolution parts, a rank histogram or a spread-skill check as well.

Every threshold carries equal weight and extreme outcomes are rare, so the average score says little about how well extremes are forecast; WeatherBench 2 notes that the CRPS does not specifically focus on extreme weather. Averaging only over cases in which an extreme occurred does not repair this and can discredit skilful forecasters (Lerch et al. 2017); claims about warnings of extremes need a threshold-weighted CRPS that emphasises the tails.

It scores one quantity at one place and lead time at a time, so it does not test whether a forecast gets the relationships between places, times or variables right. WeatherBench 2 notes that its CRPS results ignore spatial and temporal correlation, and found models trained on each wind component separately biased in wind speed; claims about joint quantities, such as rainfall totalled over a catchment, need a multivariate score such as the energy score.

The score is in the units of the forecast quantity and grows with how variable that quantity is, so raw values cannot be compared or pooled across variables, locations or seasons with different variability, and averages are dominated by the most variable cases. Comparisons across these need a skill score relative to a stated reference forecast, and the choice of reference, such as climatology or persistence, changes the result.

For an ensemble, the usual estimate treats the members as the whole forecast distribution, which penalises small ensembles: if two systems draw members from the same distribution, the one with fewer members scores worse on average. Ferro (2014) showed the usual ensemble CRPS is unfair in this sense and gave an adjusted fair version, which libraries such as scoringrules provide; it should be used whenever ensembles of different sizes are compared.

techniques.name: Rolling-Origin Evaluation
techniques.description: Rolling-origin evaluation, also called time-series cross-validation or backtesting, estimates how accurately a forecasting model will predict the future by repeatedly recreating the position it will be in when used: trained only on data up to a point in time, it forecasts the period that follows. The evaluator chooses a first forecast origin (the last time point the model may see) late enough to leave adequate training data, fits the model on the data up to that origin, forecasts every step of a fixed horizon ahead, for example one to seven days, and records the error at each lead time against the values later observed. The origin then moves forward by one step or a block of steps and the process repeats, with the model either refitted at each origin on all the data so far or on a window of fixed length (recalibration, in Tashman's terms), or kept unchanged and simply given the new observations as inputs (updating), whichever matches how it will be maintained in service. Because every forecast uses only data from before its origin, the method avoids the leakage of future information that randomly shuffled cross-validation can cause on time-ordered data, and because it uses many test periods rather than the single one of a fixed train-test split, its result depends less on which period happened to be held out. The output is the forecast error, under whatever error measure suits the forecast, broken down by lead time and by origin date for each candidate model, which supports claims about expected accuracy on unseen future data over a stated horizon and shows how that accuracy varies across seasons and conditions.

example_use_cases.description: A regional electricity distributor deciding whether to replace its regression model for day-ahead substation demand with a gradient-boosted model evaluates both over the last two years, with an origin each day at the time forecasts are issued, a horizon of the next 48 half-hours and weekly refitting, as planned for operation. It compares error at each lead time and in each season, and switches only after finding the new model better in winter peaks as well as on average.

A national weather service's post-processing team testing a machine-learning correction for station temperature forecasts places origins every day over three years, with lead times of one to ten days, and refits the correction monthly as it would in service. Error by lead time and by month shows whether the correction still helps at the longest lead times and whether its gain in winter holds in all three winters rather than one.

A hospital's operations analysts choosing a model to forecast emergency admissions one to fourteen days ahead for staff rotas compare a seasonal statistical model with a neural network, using weekly origins over two years that include two winter peaks. They report error at the seven-day lead time the rota planners use, and keep the simpler model because the neural network's advantage disappears at that horizon.

limitations.description: Refitting at every origin multiplies training cost by the number of origins: daily origins over two years means more than 700 fits. Machine-learning forecasters are often refitted only now and then and otherwise just fed new data, which Hewamalage et al. describe as common practice; that is cheaper but measures something different, so the refit schedule in the evaluation must match the one planned for deployment or the errors do not describe the deployed system.

The time-ordered split prevents leakage only through the split itself. Scaling, smoothing, decomposition, feature selection or tuning done on the whole series before splitting, or features summarising a period not yet over at the forecast time, still let future information in. Hewamalage et al. show a model beating the best possible forecast of a random walk only because a decomposition was fitted to the whole series; every such step must be redone within each origin.

Errors from neighbouring origins share most of their training data and, for multi-step horizons, overlapping test periods, so they are correlated: an average over hundreds of origins is less precise than the count suggests, and the spread across origins is not a confidence interval. Deciding whether one model beats another needs a test designed for serially correlated forecast errors, such as the Diebold-Mariano test, not a plain comparison of average errors.

The first origins have little training data, so their errors can overstate those of a model trained on the full history, and a short series leaves few test periods and a noisy average. For purely autoregressive models (past values as the only inputs) on stationary series, whose errors show no remaining autocorrelation, Bergmeir et al. show that standard k-fold cross-validation remains valid, and Hewamalage et al. recommend it for short series as it uses the data more efficiently.

It measures how the model would have performed over the history available, not how it will perform after a change that history does not contain, such as a new tariff, a replaced sensor or an abrupt structural break; Hewamalage et al. note that no evaluation design can anticipate a break that lies only in the future. Results should be stated for the periods and conditions they cover and repeated as new data arrive.
